entry.title: Learning to Forage: Hierarchical Control of a CyberOctopus
entry.content:
An octopus searching for food faces several problems at once. It must decide where to go, coordinate arms that can bend almost anywhere along their length, and keep moving when an arm encounters an obstacle. Trying to solve every muscle command and every foraging decision together creates an enormous control problem.

The octopus's distributed nervous system suggests a useful way to divide that work. Central decisions can select a behavior, arm-level programs can organize the muscles, and local feedback can respond to contact.

In our paper, Hierarchical Control and Learning of a Foraging CyberOctopus, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Udit Halder, Seung Hyun Kim, Rhanor Gillette, Prashant G. Mehta, Mattia Gazzola, and I turn this idea into a computational framework. We combine reinforcement learning for decisions, energy shaping for arm control, and a local reflex for obstacle contact. A simulated CyberOctopus then learns to collect food using progressively more active arms.

Foraging in action

Give each level a manageable job

The hierarchy assigns different kinds of decisions to different controllers:

LevelMain questionMethod
CentralShould each active arm collect food or help move the body?A policy learned with proximal policy optimization (PPO)
ArmWhich muscle activations will bring the tip to a target?Neural network energy shaping (NN-ES)
LocalHow should the arm respond when it touches an obstacle?A contact-triggered muscle reflex acting through the compliant body

This structure lets the central policy reason in terms of useful actions while an arm controller handles the many muscle activations needed to carry them out. Each level has access to a different part of the problem.

Our simulated body has eight arms, with one, two, and finally four actively controlled in the experiments. Each arm is a tapered Cosserat rod, a continuum model that tracks deformation along a slender body. Here, we restrict each arm's motion to a plane and include two longitudinal muscle groups and one transverse group. Longitudinal activation can shorten or bend the arm; transverse contraction extends it through the model's volume-conservation assumption.

Several arm planes, combined with crawling across a horizontal substrate, allow food collection in a three-dimensional scene. Individual arms still have planar dynamics; twisting and fully three-dimensional arm motions are outside this study.

Make reaching fast enough to reuse

In Shaping Energy to Control a Muscular Octopus Arm, I described how muscle activation changes an arm's equilibrium. Energy shaping uses that connection to find activations that bring the arm toward a useful configuration.

The difficulty for foraging is computational cost. The controller must repeatedly evaluate possible targets and issue new reaching commands. Solving a fresh iterative optimization problem for every candidate would make the hierarchy expensive to run.

We therefore train a neural network to map the current muscle activation and target position to a new activation profile. Let $\alpha_0(s)$ denote the current activation, $\alpha(s)$ the proposed activation, and $q$ the target. The arm-level objective is

$$ J(\alpha;\alpha_0,q) =\int_0^{L_0}\|\alpha(s)-\alpha_0(s)\|^2\,ds +\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}\|q-x_\alpha(L_0)\|. $$

Here, $L_0$ is the arm's resting length and $x_\alpha(L_0)$ is the tip position at the equilibrium induced by $\alpha$. The first term penalizes changes in muscle activation; the second penalizes missing the target. Muscle activations remain between zero and one. The activation term is a model of control effort, not a direct measurement of biological energy consumption.

To represent continuous activation profiles with a finite network output, we expand them in a set of spatial basis functions. The network predicts the coefficients. Equilibrium mechanics and rod kinematics then determine the resulting tip position and loss.

Training uses this mechanical objective directly: it does not require a collection of optimal activation labels produced by the older solver. Once trained, the network supplies the activations in a forward pass, and the simulated arm's dynamics carry out the movement.

Across 100 random reaching cases, NN-ES and iterative energy shaping both achieve median tip errors below 1% of resting arm length. NN-ES computes solutions about 200 times faster, with slightly higher muscle activation costs. This speedup concerns the computation of arm controls; it is not a claim that the entire foraging simulation or learning process runs 200 times faster.

Build foraging from two behaviors

The central policy chooses between two behavioral primitives for each active arm:

  • Reach all: attempt to collect every food target within the arm's workspace. The arm controller estimates the activation change needed for each target, selects the least costly, and repeats from the resulting configuration.
  • Crawl: execute a predefined extension-and-contraction sequence. The arm extends, anchors its tip, and pulls the body forward by a fixed step before releasing the anchor.

Reaching uses repeated NN-ES evaluations, while crawling uses a prescribed activation pattern. The sucker effect is represented through boundary conditions rather than an explicit model of individual suckers. Food is counted as collected when the arm reaches its location.

An immediate food target is not always the best reason to stop. Crawling a little farther can bring several targets into an easier part of the workspace, allowing the arm to collect them with less effort. Learning when to make that tradeoff is the central policy's job.

The policy observes a fixed maximum number of nearby, uncollected targets within an attention region. This is a spatial selection rule that limits the input size. Target coordinates are supplied by the simulation; the study does not solve visual detection.

PPO trains the policy to balance food rewards against muscle activation costs and a penalty when all active arms choose to reach despite no food being available. The resulting behavior can delay reaching until several targets are conveniently placed, then gather them together.

What does the hierarchy change?

The single-active-arm experiment compares the learned policy, a simplified analytical Q-policy, and greedy and random high-level policies, all backed by the arm controller. An additional end-to-end PPO network learns muscle commands directly from food locations and current activation.

All four hierarchical policies outperform the tested end-to-end controller on the reported metrics. Even randomly choosing between useful behaviors benefits from having a capable arm controller underneath. The learned high-level policy performs best overall, using its choices to improve both the modeled energy return and the number of decision steps needed per food item.

This comparison supports the chosen decomposition for this task and training setup. The paper does not establish that every hierarchical method outperforms every end-to-end method, and it does not report further end-to-end benchmarks for the multiarm cases.

With two active arms, the policy can coordinate movement along two orthogonal directions. Four active arms add forward, backward, left, and right movement, making it possible to revisit missed food. In the four-arm experiment without obstacles, the learned policy collects 88% of available food on average, compared with 38% for the greedy policy.

Let contact trigger a local response

An arm reaching toward food can become stuck against an obstacle even when the target is geometrically reachable. We address this with a local reflex inspired by waves of muscle activation observed in octopus arms.

At contact, the part of the arm beyond the contact point relaxes. Toward the base, longitudinal muscles on the contacting side increase activation while the other muscles relax. This reshapes the compliant arm so that it can slide past the obstacle. When contact ends, the original muscle command resumes. The model treats the activation signals as propagating instantaneously.

The four-arm results show both the benefit and its limits:

Evaluation conditionMean fraction of food collected
No obstacles88%
Obstacles, without local reflex21%
Obstacles, with local reflex67%

The high-level policy is trained without obstacles. Adding the reflex at deployment recovers much of the lost performance without retraining that policy, although collection remains below the unobstructed result. The response handles contact locally, allowing the existing foraging decisions to remain useful.

What this teaches us about soft control

The contribution is a way to combine methods with different strengths. Reinforcement learning handles sequences of discrete decisions. A mechanics-based neural controller provides fast reaching commands. Local feedback and physical compliance respond to disturbances where they occur.

These results come from a computational model, with food's horizontal coordinates on a grid compatible with the crawl step, simplified anchoring and collection, and frictionless obstacle contact. They establish a working control strategy in that setting, while hardware performance and more general arm dynamics remain open questions.

For soft robotics, the useful design principle is to make each layer solve a problem it can handle well. A central policy can coordinate a deformable body more effectively when reliable arm behaviors and local responses are already available.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Hierarchical Control and Learning of a Foraging CyberOctopus, by Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Udit Halder, Heng-Sheng Chang, Seung Hyun Kim, Rhanor Gillette, Prashant G. Mehta, and Mattia Gazzola. The paper appeared in Advanced Intelligent Systems, 5(9), 2300088 (2023), and was first published online on June 22, 2023.

Figures 1, 3, 4, and 7 are reproduced from the published paper, with surrounding page text and original captions removed and explanatory captions supplied here. The article is © 2023 The Authors, published by Wiley-VCH GmbH under CC BY 4.0. The octopus photograph within Figure 1 is separately credited to Anneli Salo under CC BY-SA 3.0.

The paper provides code for multiarm foraging and neural network energy shaping. The BibTeX below cites the published article.

entry.title: Shaping Energy to Control a Muscular Octopus Arm
entry.content:
An octopus arm has no rigid skeleton and no small set of joints to command. It can bend along its length, extend toward an object, and twist to bring its suckers into contact. That flexibility makes the arm a compelling model for soft robots, but it also raises a difficult control question: how should its muscles work together to produce a useful shape?

In our paper, Energy-shaping control of a muscular octopus arm moving in three dimensions, Udit Halder, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Mattia Gazzola, Prashant G. Mehta, and I approach this problem through energy. We model the arm and its muscles together, then choose muscle activations that make a task-specific shape an equilibrium of the combined system.

The resulting motion comes from the arm's mechanics. Once the activation pattern is applied, elastic forces, muscle forces, inertia, and damping determine how the arm moves toward its new resting configuration. We demonstrate this approach in simulations of reaching and grasping in three dimensions.

Reaching and grasping in motion

Three muscle groups, many possible motions

The geometry of a muscle matters as much as its ability to contract. In an octopus arm, three major muscle groups turn local contraction into different kinds of deformation:

Muscle groupArrangementMain mechanical role
TransverseAcross the arm, surrounding the central nerve cordNarrows the cross-section and extends the arm through approximate volume conservation
LongitudinalAlong the arm, away from its center lineShortens the arm and produces bending when activation is uneven across its sides
ObliqueHelically around the arm, with opposite handednessProduces twisting together with other coupled deformations

We describe the arm as a Cosserat rod. At each location along its center line, the model tracks both a position and the orientation of a small material frame. This lets it describe stretching, shearing, bending, and twisting in one continuum model.

Keeping track of orientation is essential. Two configurations can have similar center lines while presenting different sides of the arm to an object. To model a grasp with the suckers facing inward, we need to control that orientation as well as position.

The implementation uses one transverse activation field, four longitudinal fields, and two oblique fields, one for each handedness. Each field can vary along the arm. The oblique fibers of the same handedness share an activation, giving seven distributed controls overall.

Muscles become part of the energy model

An elastic rod stores energy when it deforms. Its internal forces and bending or twisting moments can be obtained by differentiating that energy with respect to strain. Our key modeling step is to give the muscles a compatible description.

For muscle $m$, the paper constructs a scalar function $W^m$ whose strain derivatives generate its active force and moment. The construction incorporates the muscle's geometry and a force-length relation fitted to experimental data. Multiplying by its activation $u^m$ scales its contribution:

$$ \mathbf n^m=u^m\frac{\partial W^m}{\partial\boldsymbol\nu}, \qquad \mathbf m^m=u^m\frac{\partial W^m}{\partial\boldsymbol\kappa}. $$

Here, $\boldsymbol\nu$ describes shear and stretch, while $\boldsymbol\kappa$ describes bending and twist. The vectors $\mathbf n^m$ and $\mathbf m^m$ are the muscle's internal force and moment in the arm's local frame.

For a fixed spatial activation profile $\alpha^m(s)$, the combined potential energy becomes

$$ V(q;\alpha)=\int_0^L\left[ W^e(\varepsilon(s))+ \sum_m\alpha^m(s)W^m(s,\varepsilon(s)) \right]\,ds. $$

The notation $q$ represents the arm's position and orientation along its length, $\varepsilon=(\boldsymbol\nu,\boldsymbol\kappa)$ collects its strains, and $W^e$ is the passive elastic energy density. The muscle term is written here with its dependence on muscle strain absorbed into $\varepsilon$.

This gives us a family of energy landscapes indexed by muscle activation. It is a mechanical representation of the actuator forces; it does not measure the biological energy consumed by muscle metabolism.

Choose the equilibrium, then let the arm move

The picture at the top of this post captures the control idea. Before activation, a straight arm is at rest in its passive energy landscape. Activating the muscles reshapes that landscape, allowing a bent or twisted configuration to become a new equilibrium.

There is an important constraint: the available muscles determine which landscapes can be produced. A transverse muscle cannot apply an arbitrary sideways force, for example. In conventional energy-shaping design, reconciling a desired energy with these actuator restrictions leads to difficult equations called matching conditions.

Our muscle-energy formulation builds those restrictions into the family $V(q;\alpha)$. We search over physically available activations, with $0\leq\alpha^m(s)\leq1$, to find an equilibrium suited to the task. For the unloaded arm with a fixed base and free tip, the equilibrium condition balances active muscle loads against passive elastic loads.

The search minimizes a combination of activation effort and task error:

$$ J(\alpha,q)= \frac12\sum_m\int_0^L[\alpha^m(s)]^2\,ds +J_{\mathrm{task}}(q). $$

For reaching, the task cost penalizes tip-position and tip-orientation errors. For grasping, it encourages the arm to approach the object and face its suckers toward it, while a penalty discourages penetration. The squared-activation term regularizes muscle effort; minimizing it is not a claim of optimal metabolic efficiency.

The algorithm alternates between three steps:

  1. For the current activations, solve for equilibrium strains and reconstruct the arm from base to tip.
  2. Propagate a costate from tip to base to determine how the task objective responds to changes along the arm.
  3. Update the activations using that information, respecting their bounds, and repeat.

This is an optimal control calculation along the spatial coordinate of the arm. The pose evolves in $SE(3)$, the space of three-dimensional positions and rotations. A useful reduction expresses the costate through two three-component vectors with the interpretation of internal forces and moments.

After optimization, the activation profile is held constant in time. Muscle forces still change as the arm deforms because they depend on its current geometry and muscle lengths. With damping, the model's total mechanical energy is non-increasing along the motion. The paper uses this to argue local asymptotic stability under technical assumptions; a full functional-analytic proof for the infinite-dimensional system is left for future work.

Reaching means getting the orientation right, too

The simulated arm is 20 cm long and tapers from a base radius of 1.2 cm to a tip radius of 0.12 cm. We discretize it into 100 rod elements in Elastica.

In a representative reaching movement, transverse activation extends the distal arm, longitudinal activation near the base bends it toward the target, and oblique activation twists it to orient the suckers. The three muscle groups cooperate to meet a position-and-orientation objective.

We test 125 targets distributed within a cube of side length 20 cm. The largest position errors occur at distant corners outside the arm's reachable workspace. Targets close to the base also challenge the arm's ability to bend and twist at the same time.

The normalized orientation error stays below 0.1 in all tested cases. This is a specific matrix-based measure, $|Q^*-Q(L)|_F^2/8$, rather than an angular error in degrees or a percentage of successful reaches. The experiment shows how the controller performs across a workspace that includes physically difficult and unreachable targets.

Wrapping around an object

Grasping asks more of the arm than bringing its tip to a point. A substantial length of the arm must approach the object, curve around it, and turn its sucker-facing side inward.

We express these requirements through an objective acting on the distal 70% of the arm, together with a non-penetration penalty. Longitudinal and oblique activation then produce a spiral-like configuration around a cylindrical target.

The tests vary cylinder radius from 1 to 4 cm. Thinner cylinders are harder to wrap around: their surfaces require tighter bending, which competes with the activation-effort penalty. Separate tests keep the radius at 2 cm and vary the cylinder's tilt from $-60^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ about each of two axes.

Across those tilt tests, the position-error measure varies less than the orientation-error measure. The chosen objective places greater weight on proximity, so keeping the arm close to the cylinder can take priority over perfectly orienting the suckers.

Here, grasping means achieving the wrapping configuration in simulation. Sucker adhesion and sensing are outside this model, and the experiments do not test holding or lifting a load.

What energy shaping gives us

The contribution is a connection between anatomy, mechanics, and control design. Muscle geometry determines forces and moments; a common energy description combines them with elasticity; optimization selects activations for a useful equilibrium. The arm's dynamics then produce the transition toward that configuration.

This provides a way to coordinate a highly deformable body without prescribing the full motion of every point along it. It also keeps the actuator constraints visible throughout the design.

The demonstrated tasks involve static targets and a simulated arm. Extending the approach to moving targets, sensory feedback, and neural control requires additional work. Still, the study gives a concrete starting point for soft robotic manipulation: design how the body wants to settle, and use its mechanics to help it get there.

Paper and attribution

This post is based on Energy-shaping control of a muscular octopus arm moving in three dimensions, by Heng-Sheng Chang, Udit Halder, Chia-Hsien Shih, Noel Naughton, Mattia Gazzola, and Prashant G. Mehta. The paper appeared in Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 479(2270), 20220593 (2023).

The technical discussion and Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6 follow the arXiv:2209.04089v1 preprint, submitted September 9, 2022. The figures are reproduced in full from that version, with surrounding page text removed. The arXiv version is distributed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
